stem: A 24-year-old man has had 6 weeks of foul-smelling, greasy, watery diarrhea with bloating and a 4-kg weight loss since a hiking trip where he drank stream water. There is no blood in the stool and no fever. Stool microscopy shows pear-shaped flagellated trophozoites.
oneliner: 24M + stream water on a hike + 6 wk greasy, foul diarrhea + bloating, weight loss + no blood, no fever + pear-shaped flagellates → drug works how?
ask: The most appropriate drug works by which of the following mechanisms?

options.B: Forming toxic free radicals that damage DNA

whyNot.E: **Trimethoprim / pyrimethamine**: not first choice for this parasite

why: **Stream water + greasy, foul diarrhea + pear-shaped flagellates** = giardiasis. Drug of choice **metronidazole** is reduced inside the parasite to **free radicals that break its DNA**.

drug.name: Metronidazole
drug.how: Reduced inside anaerobes and protozoa to free radicals that damage DNA
drug.use: Giardia, Entamoeba, Trichomonas, bacterial vaginosis, C. difficile, anaerobes below the diaphragm
drug.watch: Disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol, metallic taste

stem: A 58-year-old man has had burning chest pain and regurgitation for a year. Twice-daily famotidine gave only partial relief. Endoscopy shows several confluent erosions in the lower esophagus, and he is started on omeprazole.
oneliner: 58M + 1 y burning chest pain, regurgitation + partial relief on famotidine + confluent distal esophageal erosions + omeprazole started → how does it work?
ask: Omeprazole reduces acid secretion by which of the following mechanisms?

options.A: Irreversible inhibition of the H+/K+ ATPase in parietal cells
options.B: Blocking histamine H2 receptors on parietal cells
options.C: Blocking M3 receptors on parietal cells
options.D: Activating prostaglandin E receptors on parietal cells
options.E: Neutralizing acid already in the gastric lumen

whyNot.C: **Antimuscarinics**: weak effect on acid, many side effects
whyNot.E: **Antacids**: short acting; no effect on secretion

why: **Erosive esophagitis despite an H2 blocker** calls for a PPI. **Omeprazole is activated in acid** and covalently blocks the parietal cell **H+/K+ ATPase**, the final step of acid secretion.

drug.name: Omeprazole
drug.how: Prodrug activated in acid; covalently and irreversibly inhibits the H+/K+ ATPase
drug.use: GERD, erosive esophagitis, peptic ulcers, H. pylori regimens, Zollinger-Ellison
drug.watch: Long-term: C. difficile, pneumonia, hypomagnesemia, low B12, fractures, interstitial nephritis

stem: A 26-year-old woman has had cramping lower abdominal pain for a year that eases after she passes loose stools, 3 to 4 times a day. Her blood count, CRP, celiac serology and colonoscopy are normal. She takes loperamide before her commute and the diarrhea stops.
oneliner: 26F + 1 y cramping pain eased by loose stools + normal CBC, CRP, celiac serology, colonoscopy + loperamide helps → how does it work?
ask: Loperamide helps her mainly through which of the following?

options.B: Activating mu-opioid receptors in the intestinal wall to slow motility
options.C: Binding bile acids in the intestinal lumen
options.E: Blocking muscarinic receptors on gut smooth muscle

whyNot.D: **Infliximab**: for inflammatory bowel disease; her colonoscopy is normal
whyNot.E: **Dicyclomine**: relieves cramps but is not what loperamide does

answer: Mu-opioid receptor agonism in the myenteric plexus (loperamide)
why: **Pain relieved by defecation, loose stools and normal work-up** = IBS with diarrhea. **Loperamide activates mu-opioid receptors in the gut wall**, slowing peristalsis and reducing secretions, with little CNS entry.

drug.name: Loperamide
drug.how: Mu-opioid agonist in the myenteric plexus: slows motility and secretion; poor CNS penetration
drug.watch: Constipation; toxic megacolon in colitis or C. difficile; QT prolongation at very high doses

stem: A 38-year-old man with AIDS and a CD4 count of 40/mm3 has had watery diarrhea for 3 months from cryptosporidiosis that has not responded to supportive care. He is given a subcutaneous injection of octreotide three times a day and his stool volume falls.
oneliner: 38M + AIDS, CD4 40 + 3 mo cryptosporidial diarrhea + supportive care failed + subcutaneous octreotide + stool volume falls → how does it work?
ask: Octreotide reduces his diarrhea mainly through which of the following?

options.B: Binding bile acids in the gut lumen
options.C: Activating somatostatin receptors to reduce intestinal secretion
options.D: Activating mu-opioid receptors to slow transit
options.E: Blocking muscarinic receptors on gut smooth muscle

why: **Octreotide is a long-acting somatostatin analog.** It **inhibits intestinal fluid secretion** and the release of gut hormones, which reduces stool volume in refractory secretory diarrhea.

drug.name: Octreotide
drug.how: Activates somatostatin receptors: less intestinal secretion and less hormone release
drug.use: Secretory diarrhea, VIPoma, carcinoid, acromegaly, variceal bleeding

chain: Less gut hormone release and fluid secretion

stem: A 67-year-old woman has had three episodes of right upper abdominal pain after fatty meals. Ultrasound shows several small cholesterol stones, 4 mm each, and a normal bile duct. She has severe lung disease and declines surgery. She is started on ursodiol.
oneliner: 67F + 3 episodes of biliary pain + small cholesterol stones on ultrasound + severe lung disease, no surgery + ursodiol started → how does it work?
ask: Ursodiol helps dissolve her stones mainly through which of the following?

options.B: Increasing mucus production in the gallbladder

whyNot.A: **CCK effect**: could drive stones into the duct

why: **Small cholesterol stones in a poor surgical candidate** can be dissolved. **Ursodiol** expands the bile salt pool and **lowers cholesterol secretion into bile**, so stones slowly dissolve.

drug.name: Ursodiol (also chenodiol)
drug.how: Lowers hepatic cholesterol secretion and intestinal absorption, so bile is less saturated
drug.use: Small cholesterol gallstones, primary biliary cholangitis
drug.watch: Slow (months), stones recur on stopping; chenodiol can raise liver enzymes and is teratogenic

stem: A 56-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis is brought in confused and sleepy after a night of vomiting blood. He has asterixis, and serum ammonia is elevated. Lactulose is started.
oneliner: 56M + alcohol cirrhosis + confusion after GI bleed + asterixis + high ammonia + lactulose started → how does it work?
ask: Lactulose lowers blood ammonia mainly through which of the following?

options.B: Acidifying the colon so ammonia is trapped as ammonium
options.C: Increasing urea cycle activity in the liver
options.D: Blocking GABA-A receptors in the brain
options.E: Blocking intestinal absorption of dietary protein

whyNot.C: The liver is **failing**; lactulose does not repair it
whyNot.E: Lactulose does not affect protein absorption

answer: Colonic acidification traps NH3 as NH4+ (lactulose)
why: **Cirrhosis + asterixis + high ammonia** = hepatic encephalopathy. Colonic bacteria turn **lactulose into acids**, which convert **NH3 to NH4+**; the ionized form is trapped and lost in stool.

drug.name: Lactulose
drug.how: Bacterial metabolism acidifies the colon, trapping NH4+ and flushing it out

stem: A 61-year-old woman with alcohol-related cirrhosis has ascites, spider angiomata, confusion and asterixis. Lactulose has helped only partly, and an oral antibiotic that is not absorbed from the gut is added.
oneliner: 61F + alcohol cirrhosis + ascites, spider angiomata + confusion, asterixis + partial response to lactulose + non-absorbed oral antibiotic added → how does it help?
ask: The added drug lowers her ammonia mainly through which of the following?

options.A: Trapping ammonium in an acidified colon
options.D: Blocking NMDA receptors in the brain
options.E: Reducing ammonia-producing bacteria in the colon

whyNot.B: The liver is failing; this drug does not act there
whyNot.D: Not the mechanism of an antibiotic

answer: Fewer ammonia-producing gut bacteria (neomycin or rifaximin)
why: **Hepatic encephalopathy partly controlled by lactulose.** An unabsorbed oral antibiotic such as **neomycin** (or rifaximin) **kills ammonia-producing gut bacteria**, so less ammonia reaches the blood.

drug.name: Neomycin
drug.how: Binds the 30S ribosomal subunit of gut bacteria, reducing urease-producing flora
drug.watch: Poorly absorbed orally; if absorbed: nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity

stem: A 55-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes for 20 years has early fullness after a few bites, bloating, and vomiting of food eaten many hours earlier. Endoscopy shows no obstruction, and scintigraphy shows slow emptying of a solid meal. A tablet before meals is added to speed gastric emptying. Two weeks later she reports that she cannot sit still.
oneliner: 55F + diabetes for 20 years + early fullness, bloating, vomiting of old food + no obstruction + slow gastric emptying + pre-meal tablet added + new restlessness after 2 weeks → what is the mechanism?
ask: Which of the following best describes the mechanism of the added drug?

whyNot.A: Would speed emptying but cause **cholinergic effects** such as sweating and cramps, not **restlessness**
whyNot.B: Lowers acid and does not speed **gastric emptying**, her problem
whyNot.D: Treats nausea but does not speed **gastric emptying**
whyNot.E: Protects the stomach lining and does not speed **gastric emptying**

why: A pre-meal tablet that **speeds gastric emptying** and later causes **restlessness (akathisia)** blocks dopamine D2 receptors. Removing dopamine's inhibition of the gut's cholinergic neurons increases motility; blocking D2 in the brain causes the movement side effects.

drug.name: Metoclopramide
drug.class: Prokinetic and antiemetic; dopamine D2 antagonist (also 5-HT4 agonist)
drug.how: Blocks D2 receptors on gut neurons, removing dopamine's inhibition of acetylcholine release, so gastric emptying and lower esophageal sphincter tone rise; blocks D2 in the chemoreceptor trigger zone to lessen nausea
drug.watch: Akathisia, parkinsonism, tardive dyskinesia and raised prolactin; avoid in bowel obstruction and in Parkinson disease; limit use to about 12 weeks (boxed warning for tardive dyskinesia)

idea.rule: Drugs that block D2 receptors give an antiemetic or prokinetic effect and risk extrapyramidal toxicity.
also: Prochlorperazine and haloperidol: D2 blockade with antiemetic effect and akathisia
Domperidone: peripheral D2 blocker, prokinetic, with little central toxicity because it barely enters the brain
Droperidol: D2-blocking antiemetic that can cause akathisia and QT prolongation
D2 blockade in the pituitary raises prolactin, causing galactorrhea

stem: A 31-year-old woman at 22 weeks of pregnancy has burning epigastric pain that wakes her at night and is eased by food. Endoscopy shows a 6-mm duodenal ulcer. Her obstetrician chooses a drug that is barely absorbed into the blood, works only in the acidic stomach, and is taken 1 hour before meals and apart from antacids.
oneliner: 31F + 22 weeks pregnant + night epigastric pain eased by food + 6-mm duodenal ulcer + drug barely absorbed, works only in acid, taken apart from antacids → what is the mechanism?
ask: Which of the following best describes the mechanism of the chosen drug?

options.A: Forms a sticky paste that binds the ulcer base
options.B: Irreversible inhibition of the H+/K+ ATPase pump
options.C: Blockade of histamine H2 receptors on parietal cells
options.E: Neutralization of gastric acid as a weak base

whyNot.B: Absorbed into the blood and then acts on parietal cells; the chosen drug is **barely absorbed**
whyNot.C: Absorbed into the blood and then acts on parietal cells; the chosen drug is **barely absorbed**
whyNot.D: Can stimulate uterine contractions and cause abortion, so it is avoided at **22 weeks of pregnancy**
whyNot.E: Acts at any gastric pH and does not need **an acidic stomach**

answer: Forms a sticky paste that binds the ulcer base
why: A drug that is **barely absorbed**, **needs an acidic stomach** and is separated from antacids is sucralfate. In acid it polymerizes into a sticky paste that binds the **ulcer base**, shielding it from acid and pepsin. It is safe in pregnancy because it is not absorbed.

drug.name: Sucralfate
drug.how: In acid below pH 4, cross-links into a sticky paste that binds proteins in the ulcer base, forming a barrier against acid and pepsin; barely absorbed
drug.watch: Constipation; aluminum builds up in kidney failure; binds other drugs such as levothyroxine and fluoroquinolones, so separate doses; needs acid, so it works poorly with strong acid suppression

idea.rule: Ulcer drugs act at different steps: reduce acid, neutralize acid, or protect the mucosa.
also: Proton pump inhibitors: irreversibly block the H+/K+ ATPase
H2 blockers: block histamine receptors on parietal cells
Misoprostol: prostaglandin E1 analog; contraindicated in pregnancy
Bismuth: coats the ulcer and helps kill Helicobacter pylori
